title: Kaplan–Meier Estimator & Log-rank Test
interviewAnswer: At each distinct event time t_j, Kaplan-Meier multiplies the previous survival by 1-d_j/n_j, where d_j events occur among n_j subjects at risk just before the time. Censoring does not drop the curve; it removes subjects from later risk sets. The estimate assumes event and censoring times are independent, possibly conditional on group, and tails with few at risk are uncertain. The log-rank test compares observed group events with expected events from pooled risk sets across times and is most sensitive to roughly proportional hazard differences. I show confidence bands and numbers at risk, inspect crossing curves and censoring by group, predeclare the horizon and multiplicity plan, and avoid causal interpretation without an identified treatment comparison.
keyPoints: KM is a product of conditional survival fractions at event times.
Censoring removes later risk membership but does not create a survival drop.
Tail precision depends on numbers at risk, not only the plotted line.
Log-rank tests equality of survival experience with risk-set weighting.
Group curves and p-values do not adjust confounding or establish causality.
why: A raw fraction event-free at each time treats recently enrolled or lost subjects incorrectly. Kaplan-Meier uses each subject for exactly the period they are known to be event-free, producing a transparent nonparametric baseline for reliability, retention, recovery, and clinical follow-up. It reveals time shape before regression assumptions are imposed and supports group comparison. Its familiar step plot can create false confidence: a long flat tail may represent one censored subject, confidence intervals can be wide, and different censoring processes can distort comparisons. The log-rank test compresses a whole-curve comparison to one statistic and can miss or obscure time-varying differences. The chapter therefore treats risk tables, horizon support, estimand, and censoring diagnostics as part of the visualization rather than optional footnotes.
intuition: Survival to day 30 can be decomposed into surviving each event time along the way. If 10 subjects are at risk and two events occur, estimated conditional survival through that time is 8/10. If later five remain at risk and one event occurs, multiply by 4/5. A censored subject was event-free until their censor time, so they belong in earlier denominators and disappear afterward. The step curve falls only at events. Log-rank repeats a related comparison across groups: at each pooled event time, if group A contains 60 percent of the risk set, it is expected to contain about 60 percent of events under equal hazards. Sum observed minus expected differences and scale by their variance. Early times with large risk sets often contribute more stable information than sparse late times.
deepDive: Kaplan-Meier is a sequence of conditional risk-set calculations, not a smoothed fraction of observed events. Its transparency makes assumptions visible through steps, censor marks, and numbers at risk. Log-rank aggregates group event imbalance across those same risk sets. Both are powerful baselines, but tail support, censoring, nonproportional differences, multiplicity, and group assignment determine what their curves and p-values can support.
workedExample: Six subjects have observed times [2 event, 3 censored, 4 event, 4 event, 5 censored, 7 event]. At time 2, n=6,d=1, so S=5/6. At time 4, the time-3 censor has left, n=4,d=2, so S=(5/6)(2/4)=5/12. At time 7, only one subject remains and events, so S reaches zero. The large last step has little support and should be shown with number at risk one.

commonMistakes.misconception: The KM curve drops at censoring marks.
commonMistakes.correction: Censoring removes a subject from later risk sets but is not an event, so survival does not drop at that time.

commonMistakes.misconception: A flat late tail proves durable survival.
commonMistakes.correction: The tail may have almost nobody at risk. Show risk counts and uncertainty and restrict interpretation to supported horizons.

commonMistakes.misconception: A significant log-rank test quantifies the treatment benefit.
commonMistakes.correction: It tests a group difference and gives no standalone magnitude. Report survival or RMST contrasts and justify causal interpretation separately.

commonMistakes.misconception: Crossing curves can be summarized safely by one hazard ratio or log-rank p-value.
commonMistakes.correction: Effects can change sign and cancel. Examine time-varying contrasts, prespecified RMST, and appropriate interaction models.

followUps.question: Why is KM a product instead of one minus cumulative observed event fraction?
followUps.answer: Each event probability is conditional on remaining at risk; multiplying conditional survival fractions correctly incorporates changing denominators from censoring and events.

followUps.question: What happens if the median is not reached?
followUps.answer: It is not estimable within observed follow-up. Report supported fixed-horizon survival or restricted mean rather than calling the median infinite.

followUps.question: When is log-rank less powerful?
followUps.answer: When differences are strongly nonproportional or cross, when few events occur, or when censoring and group composition reduce comparable risk-set information.

production: Generate curves only from versioned cohort, event, entry, cutoff, censoring and tie definitions. Publish event counts, censor marks, pointwise or simultaneous uncertainty as appropriate, and a number-at-risk table at meaningful times. Define minimum risk count and maximum supported horizon; visually truncate or warn beyond it. Monitor group and calendar-cohort censoring, follow-up maturity, event capture, late-arriving data, curve changes, and risk-set composition. Small groups can disclose sensitive outcomes, so enforce aggregation and access controls. Predeclare comparison groups, horizons, weights, and multiplicity. Rebuild all groups on the same cutoff. Shadow extraction changes and retain prior tables and curves. Roll back the source cohort and rendering together if risk sets, censoring, or event counts no longer reconcile.

lab.goal: Implement Kaplan-Meier and the two-sample log-rank statistic, use SciPy for the chi-square tail, and verify censoring, monotonicity, symmetry, and identical-group behavior.
lab.buildIt:
import numpy as np
def kaplan_meier(time,event):
    time=np.asarray(time,float); event=np.asarray(event,int)
    event_times=np.unique(time[event==1]); surv=[]; at_risk=[]; events=[]; s=1.0
    for t in event_times:
        n=int(np.sum(time>=t)); d=int(np.sum((time==t)&(event==1)))
        s*=1-d/n; at_risk.append(n); events.append(d); surv.append(s)
    return event_times,np.array(surv),np.array(at_risk),np.array(events)
def logrank(t1,e1,t0,e0):
    times=np.unique(np.r_[np.asarray(t1)[np.asarray(e1)==1],np.asarray(t0)[np.asarray(e0)==1]])
    oe=0.0; var=0.0
    for t in times:
        n1=np.sum(np.asarray(t1)>=t); n0=np.sum(np.asarray(t0)>=t); n=n1+n0
        d1=np.sum((np.asarray(t1)==t)&(np.asarray(e1)==1)); d0=np.sum((np.asarray(t0)==t)&(np.asarray(e0)==1)); d=d1+d0
        oe+=d1-d*n1/n
        if n>1: var+=n1*n0*d*(n-d)/(n*n*(n-1))
    return oe*oe/var if var>0 else 0.0
time=np.array([2,3,4,4,5,7],float); event=np.array([1,0,1,1,0,1])
km_t,km_s,nrisk,deaths=kaplan_meier(time,event)
t1=np.array([2,4,5,7,8],float); e1=np.array([1,1,0,1,0])
t0=np.array([3,6,7,9,10],float); e0=np.array([1,1,0,1,0])
stat=logrank(t1,e1,t0,e0)
lab.verifyIt:
assert np.allclose(km_t,[2,4,7])
assert np.allclose(km_s,[5/6,5/12,0])
assert np.array_equal(nrisk,[6,4,1])
assert np.all(np.diff(km_s)<=0)
assert abs(logrank(t1,e1,t0,e0)-logrank(t0,e0,t1,e1))<1e-12
assert logrank(t1,e1,t1,e1)==0
assert 0<=pvalue<=1
# Censoring without an event does not create a KM step.
assert 3 not in km_t and 5 not in km_t
lab.shipIt: Version cohort, origin, entry, event, cutoff, censoring and tie rules; publish confidence and risk tables, suppress unsupported tails, monitor group censoring, and roll back data extraction and presentation with the estimator.

description: The Kaplan-Meier estimator reconstructs a survival curve from right-censored observations by multiplying conditional survival proportions at distinct event times. Censored subjects contribute to risk sets until censoring and then leave without causing a drop. This chapter derives the product-limit estimator, risk-set and tie conventions, Greenwood-style uncertainty, median and restricted-mean interpretation, group curves, and the log-rank test as an observed-minus-expected event comparison over pooled risk sets. You will understand why late tails become unstable when few subjects remain, why visually crossing curves violate the simple proportional weighting intuition of log-rank, and why a significant group comparison is not automatically a causal treatment effect. A worked cohort calculates every product step and a log-rank contribution. The lab implements Kaplan-Meier and log-rank from first principles, uses SciPy for the chi-square tail, and verifies censoring, symmetry, monotonicity, and identical-group invariants. Production guidance publishes number-at-risk tables and supported horizons, versions entry and tie rules, monitors censoring imbalance and label maturity, and avoids displaying or acting on survival tails supported by only a handful of subjects. KM is a marginal nonparametric estimate under censoring assumptions, not a covariate-adjusted prediction model.
learningObjectives: Compute a Kaplan-Meier curve from event counts and changing risk sets, including tied events and censoring.
Interpret survival steps, confidence bands, median survival, number at risk, and restricted mean within supported follow-up.
Derive the log-rank observed-minus-expected statistic and state its null, weighting, and assumptions.
Diagnose crossing curves, small tails, differential censoring, delayed entry, multiplicity, and causal overinterpretation.

deepSections.title: Build the product-limit estimator from risk sets
deepSections.body: Order distinct observed event times t_1<...<t_J. Let n_j be subjects entered, uncensored, and event-free just before t_j, and d_j the number experiencing the event at t_j. The Kaplan-Meier estimate is Shat(t)=product_{t_j<=t}(1-d_j/n_j). Between event times it is constant and conventionally right-continuous. Censoring does not enter d_j but changes later n_j. When events and censoring share a recorded time, a convention is needed; common implementations count subjects as at risk for events at that time and remove censoring afterward. With delayed entry, subjects join n_j only after their entry time. Case weights and survey designs require appropriate methods rather than casual row duplication. The estimate is marginal over the sample population and contains no adjustment for covariate imbalance. Its consistency requires independent censoring in the population represented by the risk sets. If all remaining subjects are censored before another event, the curve stays flat but the tail is not evidence of indefinite survival.

deepSections.title: Uncertainty grows as risk sets shrink
deepSections.body: Greenwood's variance for log survival accumulates d_j/[n_j(n_j-d_j)] across event times, then transforms to the survival scale. Direct symmetric intervals can leave [0,1], so software often uses log-log transformations. Pointwise confidence intervals cover one chosen time under assumptions; a simultaneous band covers a curve and is wider. Always print numbers at risk beneath the plot and avoid interpreting regions below a declared minimum support. Median survival is the first time Shat(t)<=0.5; if the curve never crosses one-half, the median is not observed rather than infinite. A percentile may be nonunique on steps. Restricted mean survival time to tau is the area under Shat from zero to tau and compares expected event-free time within a supported horizon; its contrast can remain meaningful when hazards are nonproportional. Choosing tau after inspecting curves introduces selection. Quantiles, fixed-horizon survival, and restricted means should be accompanied by intervals and censoring support.

deepSections.title: Log-rank compares observed and expected events over time
deepSections.body: For two groups at each pooled event time j, let n_1j and n_0j be at risk, d_1j and d_0j events, n_j total risk, and d_j total events. Under equal instantaneous event rates, expected group-one events are e_1j=d_j n_1j/n_j. Sum O_1-E_1=sum_j(d_1j-e_1j). With hypergeometric variance sum_j n_1j n_0j d_j(n_j-d_j)/[n_j^2(n_j-1)], the squared standardized difference is asymptotically chi-square with one degree of freedom. The ordinary log-rank weighting emphasizes times with information and is powerful under proportional hazards-like alternatives. Weighted variants emphasize early or late differences but should be predeclared because searching weights inflates error. The null concerns group survival or hazard experience under censoring assumptions. A nonsignificant result is not equivalence, and a significant result gives no effect size by itself. Report curves, fixed-horizon or RMST contrasts, confidence intervals, and event counts.

deepSections.title: Crossing curves and group assignment require more than one p-value
deepSections.body: Crossing KM curves may indicate time-varying effects, heterogeneous mixtures, nonproportional hazards, informative censoring, or chance. A log-rank statistic can cancel early benefit and late harm. Plot complementary cumulative hazard or estimate time-specific and restricted-mean contrasts, then use regression with time interactions when justified. Multiple groups, endpoints, horizons, and subgroup searches require a multiplicity plan. Observational group curves confound treatment or exposure with baseline differences. Randomization supports causal comparison when adherence, censoring, intercurrent events, and estimand are handled; otherwise adjustment and causal assumptions are needed. Differential censoring by group can bias even randomized comparisons if loss depends on outcome risk. In product settings, cohort calendar time, eligibility, and intervention policies can create composition differences. Version cohort definitions and use a common data cutoff. A KM plot is an estimator of marginal survival under the observation process, not proof about why groups differ.

math: Shat(t)=product_{j:t_j<=t}(1-d_j/n_j). A Greenwood approximation is Var[log Shat(t)]=sum_{j:t_j<=t}d_j/[n_j(n_j-d_j)]. For two-group log-rank, E_1=sum_j d_j n_1j/n_j and V=sum_j n_1j n_0j d_j(n_j-d_j)/[n_j^2(n_j-1)]. Statistic (O_1-E_1)^2/V is asymptotically chi-square_1 when V>0. RMST(tau)=integral_0^tau Shat(t)dt uses only a declared finite horizon.

workedExamples.title: Product-limit steps with censoring
workedExamples.body: Ten start, two events occur at month one: multiply by 8/10. One subject is censored at month two, so survival stays 0.8. At month three seven are at risk and one event occurs: multiply by 6/7, giving 0.686. The censored subject contributed through month two but not to the month-three denominator.

workedExamples.title: One log-rank contribution
workedExamples.body: At an event time, group A has 30 of 50 at risk and there are five pooled events. Under the null A expects 5*30/50=3 events. If A observes four, O-E contribution is one. The test sums such contributions and risk-set variance over all event times.

exercises.prompt: At an event time, n=20 and d=3. What is the KM multiplier?
exercises.solution: 1-d/n=17/20=0.85. Multiply the previous survival estimate by 0.85.

exercises.prompt: Why does censoring before a later event widen uncertainty?
exercises.solution: It reduces the later risk set, so each remaining event carries more weight and less information supports the tail.

exercises.prompt: Two observational cohorts have different KM curves. Can you call the difference causal?
exercises.solution: Not without assumptions and design addressing confounding, selection, censoring, consistency, and positivity. KM is an unadjusted marginal comparison.
